sentences.text: Last week we drew the demand curve. Today we ask a different question: how much does demand move when the price moves?
That is what economists call the price elasticity of demand, and it is probably the most useful number in this whole course.
Take coffee on campus. If the café raises the price by ten percent and sales drop by only three percent, demand is inelastic.
People grumble, but they keep buying, because there is no other coffee within a five-minute walk of the lecture halls.
Now think about one particular brand of sparkling water. Raise the price by ten percent and people simply pick up a different brand from the same shelf.
Sales might fall by twenty percent or more. That is elastic demand.
So what makes the difference? Mostly, whether there is a close substitute, and how much of your budget the thing takes up.
Salt is a classic example. Even if the price doubled, you would barely notice, so you would keep buying the same amount.
Rent is the opposite. It is a huge share of the budget, so people move, take a roommate, or commute further when it goes up.
Time matters too. In the short run, people can't change much. Give them a year, and they find alternatives.
Write this down, because it will be on the midterm: substitutes, share of budget, and time. Those three explain most of what you will see.

Sure. Right now about a third of new users drop off at the permission screen, before they've recorded anything at all.

I'd ship the copy change this week. It's one string, and it buys us time to do the redesign properly.
Agreed. Marcus, how does that affect the offline work on your side?
It doesn't, really. Offline mode is mostly sync and storage, and the hard part is conflict handling when two devices edit the same note.
We have a design for it, but I want two more weeks of testing on real devices before I'd call it done.
Two weeks is fine. What I don't want is another quarter where we find the problems after launch.
Then let's put a hard rule on it: no launch until we've run the full sync test on four devices for a week.
Good. So the plan for the quarter is the copy change this week, offline mode by the end of November, and the onboarding redesign in December.
One thing I'd add: let's interview five users who dropped off, so the redesign isn't based only on numbers.

Will do. I'll include the two-device conflict cases we found last month.
Great. Let's stop there. Thanks, everyone.
Good morning, everyone. Let's pick up where we left off on Tuesday.
We said that a demand curve shows how much people want to buy at every possible price, holding everything else constant.
Today I want to talk about what happens when something other than the price changes, because that is where most real-world questions live.
Say incomes go up across the whole economy. At every single price, people now buy a little more than before.
So the whole curve shifts to the right. We are not moving along the curve, we are drawing a new one.
Does that work the same way for everything we buy?
Good question. Not quite. For most goods, yes. We call those normal goods, and they are the case you should assume by default.
But for some goods, like instant noodles or bus tickets, people buy less when they earn more, because they switch to something they like better.
Those are inferior goods. The name sounds like a judgment, but it is only a description of how demand responds to income.
Prices of related goods matter too. If coffee gets expensive, demand for tea goes up. Those two are substitutes.
If printers get cheaper, people buy more ink. Those two are complements, and their demand curves move in the opposite direction.
Then there are expectations. If everyone believes prices will rise next month, demand jumps today, before anything has actually changed.
So a change in price moves us along the curve, and everything else shifts it?
Exactly. That is the single most important distinction in this chapter, and it is the one people get wrong on the exam.
Let me give you a quick test. The price of a concert ticket goes up, and fewer people buy tickets. Is that a shift or a movement?
A movement along the curve, because only the price changed.
Right. Now a famous band announces a tour, and more people want tickets at every price. That one is a shift.
For next week, read chapter four on elasticity, and try the first five problems at the end of the chapter.
We will start Thursday with a short quiz on shifts versus movements along the curve, so make sure you are comfortable with today's examples.
Any questions before we wrap up? No? Then see you on Thursday.
Let's hear from the Mexico City team. How did the launch campaign go?
Muy bien. En las primeras dos semanas tuvimos casi el doble de descargas que en Brasil.
Twice as many downloads? What do you think made the difference?
Creo que fue el precio. Lo bajamos a cuarenta y nueve pesos, and we kept the free trial for the first month.
That's a useful case. Elasticity again: a small price cut, a big jump in demand.
Exacto. Pero también cambiamos los anuncios. Usamos videos cortos de estudiantes reales en lugar de actores.
So you changed two things at once. How do you know which one did the work?
Honestly, we don't know yet. We are running a test next month with the old price and the new videos.
Good. That is exactly the kind of answer I want to see in your final reports: what you changed, and how you'll separate the effects.
